# The example

This vignette walks through the annotation of one feature group step by step,
using the low-level functions that `annotateAdducts()` is built from. The
group holds the ions of **2-furoylglycine** (C~7~H~7~NO~4~,
M = 169.0375 Da), a marker of coffee intake, measured in positive mode in a
coffee intervention study. All eight features elute within 0.2 s and their
intensities correlate across the study samples, so `groupFeatures()` put them
in one group.

```{r data}
#| message: false
library(IonFamilies)
library(dplyr)

mz <- c(95.0124, 124.0392, 152.0342, 170.0445, 171.0496, 192.0275,
        377.0300, 393.0019)
int <- c(71.6, 81.4, 49.8, 100, 4.33, 11.3, 1.76, 1.82)
grp <- rep("FG.1", length(mz))
```

# Step 1: isotopes

Heavy isotopologues are not adducts, so they are found first and left out of
the voting. `MetaboCoreUtils::isotopologues()` checks that the mass
difference fits an isotope step *and* that the intensity ratio is plausible
for a molecule of that mass.

```{r isotopes}
iso <- annotateIsotopes(mz, IsotopologueParam(), intensity = int,
                        groups = grp)
data.frame(mz, int, iso)
```

m/z 171.050 is the ¹³C isotopologue of m/z 170.045 (4 % of its intensity,
about what seven carbons give).

# Step 2: implied neutral masses

A rule describes how an ion is formed from `nmol` neutral molecules: its
charge and the mass that is added or lost (`massdiff`). Inverting it gives the
neutral mass a feature would have *if* it were that ion:

$$M = \frac{|z| \cdot m/z - \Delta m}{n_{mol}}$$

```{r rules}
rules <- defaultAdductRules("positive")
some <- rules %>%
    filter(name %in% c("[M+H]+", "[M+Na]+", "[M+H-H2O]+", "[M+H-HCOOH]+",
                       "[2M+K]+"))
some %>%
    select(name, nmol, charge, massdiff, quasi, ips)
round(impliedMasses(mz, some), 4)
```

Read the table column by column. The value 169.037 appears for m/z 170.045
as `[M+H]+`, for 192.028 as `[M+Na]+`, for 152.034 as `[M+H-H2O]+`, for
124.039 as `[M+H-HCOOH]+` and for 377.030 as `[2M+K]+`. Five features agree
on one neutral mass.

# Step 3: voting

`neutralMassVote()` automates that reading for all rules:

1. Every feature is tried as every **quasi-molecular** ion (rules with
   `quasi == 1`, such as `[M+H]+` and `[M+Na]+`). Each try is an *anchor*
   and gives a candidate neutral mass.
2. A candidate becomes a **hypothesis** when at least one *other* feature is
   explained by some rule as an ion of the same mass (within `ppm` +
   `mzabs`).
3. Hypotheses found from different anchors but with the same members are
   merged.
4. Hypotheses are **ranked** by the summed rule score (`ips`, higher for
   common ions) and then by the intensity they explain.

```{r vote}
keep <- !isIsotopologue(iso)
votes <- neutralMassVote(mz[keep], int[keep], rules)
votes %>%
    mutate(mz = mz[keep][feature]) %>%
    select(hypothesis, M, n_ions, score, mz, adduct) %>%
    head(12)
```

Hypothesis 1 is furoylglycine with five supporting ions. The later
hypotheses are coincidences: with `r nrow(rules)` rules, most pairs of m/z
values can be connected by *some* pair of rules.

# Step 4: keep all hypotheses or only the best?

CAMERA reported, for each feature, only hypotheses that did not conflict with
better ones. `bestHypotheses()` reproduces that choice:

```{r best}
hints <- annotateAdducts(mz, AdductVoteParam(), intensity = int,
                         groups = grp, exclude = !keep)
bestHypotheses(hints) %>%
    mutate(mz = mz[feature]) %>%
    select(mz, M, adduct, n_ions)
```

*IonFamilies* keeps **all** hypotheses by default, ranked per feature. A
true annotation that ranks second for a feature is then still visible.
Missing a true relationship costs more than showing an extra suggestion,
because annotations are hints to be checked. `nBest` limits how many are
written to text:

```{r format}
data.frame(mz, iso,
           best_only = formatAdducts(hints, nBest = 1, nFeatures = length(mz)),
           top_three = formatAdducts(hints, nBest = 3, nFeatures = length(mz)))
```

# Why the grouping matters

Because a long rule list connects almost anything, voting is only meaningful
inside groups of features that are already known to belong together: same
retention time, correlated intensities across samples, similar peak shapes.
That evidence comes from `groupFeatures()`. *IonFamilies* adds the chemical
interpretation on top. Good groups give good hints.
